target_concept: Explain why the length of the smallest string bounds the maximum possible LCP length.

mcq.questionText: Why does the length of the smallest string bound the maximum possible length of the longest common prefix (LCP) among a set of strings?
options: The longest common prefix cannot exceed the length of the smallest string because any longer prefix would require characters beyond the end of that string.
The longest common prefix is limited by the average length of all strings, since longer strings dominate the comparison.
Processing characters beyond the smallest string length can cause array index out-of-bounds errors, so the algorithm must stop at that point.
The longest common prefix is always equal to the length of the shortest string, regardless of the actual characters.
mcq.correctAnswer: The longest common prefix cannot exceed the length of the smallest string because any longer prefix would require characters beyond the end of that string.
mcq.explanation: A common prefix must be present in every string. If a prefix were longer than the smallest string, it would contain characters that the smallest string does not have, making it impossible for all strings to share that prefix. Therefore, the LCP length is bounded by the length of the smallest string.
